raw.etymology_text:
Inherited from Middle High German sīn, from Old High German sīn (“to be”), from Proto-West Germanic *sīn, an analogical infinitive formed within the suppletive paradigm of “to be” from forms ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be, exist”).
It replaced the older infinitive wesan, from *wesaną (“to be, remain”). The paradigm is additionally suppleted with forms from *beuną (“to be, exist, become”).
Cognate with Dutch zijn (“to be”), Low German sien (“to be”).
